extracted.intended_audience: authors and typists typesetting mathematical documents with TeX (plain TeX users)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and best practices for producing high-quality mathematical typography using (plain) TeX, covering punctuation, spacing, font choices, delimiters, ellipses, line-breaking, and related macros.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation placement with inline vs display math
rubrics_metrics.description: When a formula is followed by a period, comma, semicolon, colon, question mark, exclamation point, etc., put the punctuation after the $ when the formula is in the text; but put the punctuation before the $$ when the formula is displayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TEX’s spacing rules work best when punctuation marks are not considered part of formulas. Example: If $x<0$, we have shown that $$y=f(x).$$

rubrics_metrics.name: Segregate formulas from running text
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep math properly segregated in paragraphs: don’t take operators like − and = outside of the $’s, and keep commas inside the formula only if they are truly part of the formula; punctuation that belongs linguistically to the sentence should be left outside the $’s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t type ‘$x = a, b$’; instead type ‘$x = a$, $b$, or $c$’ or use a tie: ‘or~$c$’. This avoids unequal spacing and bad line-break behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ties (~) to prevent bad line breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert ties (nonbreaking spaces) to prevent undesirable line breaks between math and surrounding text or between items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ‘or~$c$’ and using ‘$a_i$,~$a_{i+1}$’ when needed. See exercises and examples throughout chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Math-surround spacing (mathsurround)
rubrics_metrics.description: TEX inserts additional space before and after each formula determined by \mathsurround; plain TeX sets \mathsurround=0pt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can change \mathsurround (e.g., \mathsurround=1pt) to get visual separation similar to traditional typewriter practice. The value in force when TEX reads the closing $ is used at both sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set common mathematical functions in roman type
rubrics_metrics.description: Common mathematical function names (log, sin, cos, lim, etc.) should be set in roman type, not italic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plain TEX defines 32 control sequences for this purpose (\sin, \cos, \lim, \log, \Pr, \max, \min, \inf, \sup, \det, \gcd, etc.). Use these macros so they have correct spacing and (for some) operator-limit behavior in display style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large operators get limits in display style
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain operators (\det, \gcd, \inf, \lim, \liminf, \limsup, \max, \min, \Pr, \sup) behave like large operators in display style so that their subscripts/superscripts can become limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \max_{1\le n\le m} and \lim_{x\to0} produce the conventional limit placement in displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining or one-shot roman names
rubrics_metrics.description: If a needed roman operator is not provided, define a new control sequence or use \rm (or an \hbox) for a one-shot roman rendering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $\sqrt{{\rm Var}(X)}$, $x_{\rm max}-x_{\rm min}$. Be aware that \hbox contents do not scale for subscripts and use the current font; use \hbox{\rm ...} if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: \bmod versus \pmod usage
rubrics_metrics.description: \bmod is for 'mod' used as a binary operator between quantities; \pmod is for parenthesized 'mod' at the end of a congruence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: \gcd(n,m\bmod n) and x\equiv y+1\pmod{m^2} (\pmod inserts parentheses automatically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Font switches within math (\bf, \cal, \mit, \it, \sl, \tt)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use font switches to get boldface, calligraphic, math italic, text italic, slanted, or typewriter letters in math, but be mindful of their domain and side effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: \cal affects only uppercase A–Z; \bf produces bold roman for characters A–Z,a–z,0–9 and certain Greek and accents; \mit affects uppercase Greek; \it is text italic and better for actual italic words inside math; \it, \sl, \tt are text-size fonts and should not be used in subscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid \hbox for font changes in subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Material placed in an \hbox is typeset in the same size regardless of script level and uses the current font, so it can produce unintended results in subscripts or when surrounding text has different font shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example pitfalls: $x_{\hbox{max}}$ yields non-scaled text; in slanted theorem statements \hbox without \rm may inherit slanted font. Use \rm inside \hbox if needed: \hbox{\rm Var}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing between formulas in displays (\quad, \qquad)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \quad (one em) and \qquad (two ems) to insert traditional inter-formula spacing such as between an equation and a side condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: $$F_n = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2},\qquad n\ge2.$$ \quad is independent of math size/family and is the usual spacing for display-side conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate adjacent inline formulas with words or explicit spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulas in text should be separated by words (preferred) or explicit spaces/ties; avoid clustering formulas separated only by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If forced to separate formulas, insert an explicit interword space (e.g., use '\ '), example: ... $F_n=F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}$,\ $n\ge2$.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine-grained spacing within formulas (\, \> \; \!)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use thin (\,), medium (\>), thick (\;) and negative thin (\!) spaces to fine-tune intersymbol spacing when TeX's automatic rules are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical sizes: \,, \>, \;, \! correspond to predefined mu-based skips. Use these rarely, only after examining proofs. Use \mskip and \mkern for explicit mu units (e.g., \mskip 9mu plus 2mu or \mkern18mu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use thin space before differential 'dx' and in other conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert a thin space before dx, dy, etc. in integrals and differential expressions for better visual separation: f(x)\,dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $\int_0^\infty f(x)\,dx$, $y\,dx-x\,dy$, $dx\,dy=r\,dr\,d\theta$. No thin space is needed when dt appears alone as numerator in a fraction (\int_1^x dt/t).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical units: roman type and thin space
rubrics_metrics.description: When physical units appear in formulas they should be set in roman type and separated from the preceding material by a thin space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insert thin space after factorials when followed by letter/number/opening delimiter
rubrics_metrics.description: After an exclamation point used as factorial, insert a thin space if the next character is a letter, number, or opening delimiter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $(2n)!/\bigl(n!\,(n+1)!\bigr)$ and displayed combinatorial coefficients should have a thin space: $${52!\over13!\,13!\,26!}$$

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \, and \! to correct optical spacing glitches
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply positive (\,) or negative (\!) thin spaces to open up or close up awkward visual gaps created by certain symbol combinations (sqrt signs, superscripts next to slashes, multiple integrals, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: $\sqrt{\,\log x}$, $x^2\!/2$, $n/\!\log n$, $\int\!\!\!\int_D dx\,dy$; exercise judgment at proof stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and use TeX’s atom types and spacing table
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX converts formulas to math lists of atoms of types Ord, Op, Bin, Rel, Open, Close, Punct, and Inner; spacing between adjacent atoms is determined by a table mapping pairs to no/thin/medium/thick space (0/1/2/3). Parenthesized entries apply only in display/text styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing which constructs produce which atom types (e.g., fractions -> Inner) helps predict and control spacing. Appendix G and the table in the chapter give the precise rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delimiter macros affect atom types (\bigl, \bigr, \bigm, \big vs \left ... \right)
rubrics_metrics.description: \bigl, \bigr, \bigm, and \big produce delimiters that differ in the atom types they generate (Open, Close, Rel, Ord respectively) and thus can change spacing; \left and \right enclose a subformula that becomes an Inner atom which may produce different spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ord followed by Inner (from \left) gets a thin space, but Ord followed by Open (from \bigl) does not. Use the appropriate delimiter command to get desired spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \left and \right for vertical bars and similar delimiters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters like '|' are treated as ordinary symbols (leading to wrong spacing) unless used with \left and \right; using \left|...\right| ensures correct delimiter semantics and spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: $|-x|=|+x|$ has wrong spacing; use $\left|-x\right|=\left|+x\right|$.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses: use \ldots for low dots and \cdots for centered dots
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose \ldots (three low dots) or \cdots (three centered dots) according to mathematical context: \cdots between +, −, ×, =, ≤, ⊂ and similar relations; \ldots between commas and in juxtaposition without operators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $x_1+\cdots+x_n$, $f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$, $x_1x_2\ldots x_n$. At end of formula or before closing delimiter, add a thin space (e.g., \cdots\, or \ldots\,) or use \dots in text which abbreviates $\ldots\,$.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line breaking in paragraph formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX may break formulas between lines only after an outer-level relation (=, <, →) or after an outer-level binary operation (+, −, ×). Commas in formulas never allow breaks; breaks are governed by penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To forbid a break, use braces to box subformulas or insert \nobreak; to permit a break at a chosen point use \allowbreak. A discretionary multiplication sign '\*' can allow a break with an inserted × at the break.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties controlling math line breaks (\relpenalty, \binoppenalty, \penalty, \nobreak)
rubrics_metrics.description: \relpenalty is the penalty for breaking after a Rel atom (default 500), \binoppenalty for Bin atoms (default 700). You can override by inserting \penalty<number> or use \nobreak (abbrev for \penalty10000) to prohibit breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert '\penalty<number>' immediately after the atom to set a per-case penalty. Plain TeX defaults are \relpenalty=500, \binoppenalty=700.

rubrics_metrics.name: Braces and set-builder notation: use \{ \} and \mid with thin spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \{ and \} for set delimiters; for set-builder expressions use \mid for the vertical bar and insert thin spaces inside the braces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $\{a,b,c\}$, $\{\,x\mid x>5\,\}$ or $\{\,x:x>5\,\}$. The colon alternative is acceptable (\:), but \mid with thin spaces is recommended for clarity.
